lines.text: A small kingdom on the edge of Europe that sent its ships around the world. This is the story of Portugal, from Roman Lusitania to today.
Long before Portugal, the Romans made the west of Iberia a province and named it Lusitania, after the Lusitanian people who had fought them.
In the twelfth century, Afonso Henriques broke free of the kingdom of Leon and became the first king of Portugal.
By 1143 his kingdom was recognised, making Portugal one of the oldest nation states in Europe.
In 1385, at Aljubarrota, the Portuguese defeated Castile and kept their kingdom independent.
A year later Portugal sealed an alliance with England at Windsor. It is still in force, the oldest alliance in the world.
In 1394 Prince Henry was born, later called the Navigator. He sent ship after ship down the coast of Africa, though he rarely sailed himself.
In 1415 Portugal captured Ceuta in North Africa, the first step of the first global European empire, which would last until Macau was handed back in 1999.
Pedro Alvares Cabral, bound for India in 1500, sailed so far west that he reached Brazil and claimed it for Portugal.
Just before, in 1498, Vasco da Gama had sailed round Africa to Calicut in India, opening a sea road to Asia and its riches.
The wealth of the spice trade paid for the Jeronimos Monastery in Lisbon, where da Gama himself now lies.
Downriver, the Belem Tower guarded the Tagus, the place from which the ships set out for the Indies.
Luis de Camoes, who sailed east himself, wrote The Lusiads, the great epic poem of the voyages.
In 1580 the royal line failed, and for sixty years Portugal shared a king with Spain, until it won back its own crown in 1640.
On All Saints' Day in 1755 a huge earthquake, then a tsunami and fires, destroyed much of Lisbon and shook the thinking of all Europe.
In the old quarters of Lisbon and Coimbra, a new music was born, fado, sad songs full of longing.
In 1822 the prince Pedro declared Brazil independent and became its emperor. Portugal had lost the jewel of its empire.
Antonio de Oliveira Salazar, born in 1889, would rule Portugal as a dictator for over thirty years and cling to its colonies in Africa.
In 1904 Benfica was founded in Lisbon. With Eusebio, it would win the European Cup twice in the early sixties.
On the fifth of October 1910 a revolution ended the monarchy, and Portugal became a republic.
In 1922 Jose Saramago was born, the novelist who would win the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1998.
Luis Montenegro was born in 1973. In 2024 he would become prime minister.
In April 1974, soldiers ended the dictatorship almost without a shot, and people put carnations in their rifles. Democracy came, and the African colonies went free.
In 1985 Cristiano Ronaldo was born in Madeira. He would become one of the highest scorers in football history.
In 1986 Portugal and Spain joined the European Community, and Portugal turned its face to Europe.
In 1998 Lisbon hosted the world's fair, Expo 98, devoted to the oceans that had made the country's name.
And in 2016, with Ronaldo as captain, Portugal won the European Championship for the first time.
From a frontier kingdom to the ends of the Earth and back, Portugal still looks out to sea.
